entry.hook: He Xiangu (a Xian who never sought immortality through struggle, but simply forgot to die) is the only woman among the Eight Immortals—and perhaps the most quietly unsettling figure in the entire fellowship. Her legend carries no thunder, no sword, no cosmic rebellion. She was a peasant girl who ate a peach, lost her hunger, and never looked back. The real question her story asks is not how she cheated death, but whether she ever felt the need to escape it at all.

body.body_1:
纯阳仙姑 / Immortal Maiden He (He Qiong) / Birth Name: 何琼 (He Qiong)
Affiliation: 八仙，女仙一脉 (The Eight Immortals, Female Immortal Tradition)
Birth Era: Tang Dynasty (circa 7th century CE, legends lacking precise dating)
Place of Origin: 广州增城 (Zengcheng, Guangdong Province, present-day China)
Cultivation Site: 罗浮山 (Luofu Mountain, a sacred Daoist peak in Guangdong)
Current Realm: 真仙 (Zhen Xian — a True Immortal, fully ascended beyond the Three Realms and the Five Phases, seated among the Eight Immortals)
body.body_2: He Xiangu has achieved the state of a Zhen Xian (True Immortal), fully ascended beyond the reach of the Three Realms and the Five Phases, no longer subject to the karmic debt cycle. The sources do not preserve a full stage-by-stage cultivation record for her, as her path diverged sharply from the conventional framework of Lian Qi, Zhu Ji, Jin Dan, and Yuan Ying. Her legend does not depict her facing the San Zai (Three Calamities) or the process of excising the San Shi (Three Worms). Instead, her ascension is presented as a gentle, almost accidental outcome of a pure heart and a gift of celestial food. Her current peril, if it can be called that, is not the terror of the tribulation but the quiet loneliness of a woman who outlived every mortal she knew, carrying no bitterness and no visible regret.
body.body_3: (1) Dao Gate — He Xiangu's entrance into the immortal path was not born of a cataclysmic event or a conscious decision to defy mortality. According to the most widely circulated account, she was a young woman from a farming family in Zengcheng, Guangdong. In her youth, she encountered an immortal being—sometimes identified as a mysterious old woman, sometimes as one of the Eight Immortals in disguise—who offered her a peach from a celestial orchard. She ate it, and from that day forward, she no longer felt hunger. Later legends enrich the story: during a dream, a spirit taught her to consume Yun Mu (云母, mica powder), a substance said to grant lightness and longevity. The tradition does not record her first experience of absorbing Qi as a violent or terrifying process, unlike the stark accounts of conventional cultivators. Instead, it emphasizes a quiet, gradual transformation: she could run like a galloping horse, scale cliffs with ease, and spend days in the mountains gathering herbs without food or water. (2) Fear at initiation — The classic texts offer no scene of her feeling that her body was being poisoned or her spirit shattered. The absence of such detail may itself be significant: He Xiangu's path was not one of struggle against the Dao, but of alignment with it. (3) Mortal bonds at the time of entry — She was the daughter of a farming family, likely of modest means. The later legend of her being summoned to court by Empress Wu Zetian suggests she was known as a local curiosity before her full transcendence. She was never a wife, a mother, or a court official; the role of "daughter" was her primary mortal identity. After her transformation, she continued to live among her family for a time, still recognizable, still called by her birth name. The separation was gradual, not abrupt.
body.body_4: The tradition does not present He Xiangu as having undergone the canonical Zhu Ji process—the deliberate shutdown of mortal metabolism through painful internal alchemy. Her Bi Gu (abstention from grain) was an organic consequence of eating the celestial peach and ingesting the Yun Mu, not the result of a violent struggle against her own body. (1) Physical transformation — She simply stopped feeling hunger. Her digestive functions quietened of their own accord, and the ritualized pain of the standard cultivator's "metabolic death" is absent from her lore. (2) Emotional detachment — The legend emphasizes her serene, unflappable nature from the beginning. She is not described as losing the ability to feel sorrow or love through a traumatic excision; rather, these emotions seem to have naturally receded as her clarity deepened. One of the most striking details is that when she returned to her village after her transformation, she could walk through the market without being recognized by any of her former neighbors. Whether this was due to her physical lightness altering her appearance, or something subtler—the unseen veil that settles between a woman who has stopped aging and the people who have continued doing so—the legend leaves unspoken. (3) The gap — There is no recorded moment of her standing before a family grave unable to cry. The tradition presents her as fundamentally placid; that placidity may be both her gift and her silent price.
body.body_5: He Xiangu's path did not involve the formation of a Jin Dan (Golden Core) through the violent compression of Xian Tian Yi Qi. Her body was not reforged as a karmic singularity. Instead, her longevity was granted through the consumption of celestial substances—the peach and the Yun Mu—which gradually altered her physiology without the standard internal furnace of Ni Lian Yin Yang. (1) The absence of the core — There is no record of her experiencing the terror of a newly condensed Golden Core, no moment of realizing she had become a target for the Dao's immune response. She did not accumulate a debt through theft; she received her longevity as a gift, which, within the logic of the mythic framework, may be why the San Zai do not target her. She owes the cosmos nothing because she took nothing by force. (2) No recorded calamities — The classic texts do not describe her enduring Yin Huo, Bi Feng, or thunder tribulations. Her path is presented as one of protection and blessing, not resistance and punishment. (3) The weight of debt — If the conventional Xian is a cosmic thief, He Xiangu is the exception: a woman who was given what others had to steal. The tradition does not explore whether she felt the burden of her immortality differently because of this, but the implication is that her lightness—both physical and spiritual—was not merely a cultivation achievement but a lived experience of existing outside the standard karmic economy.
body.body_6: The tradition does not describe He Xiangu undergoing the ritualized excision of the San Shi (Three Worms). There is no record of her severing greed, anger, or lust through an act of deliberate self-dismemberment of the spirit. However, her character as depicted in the Eight Immortals corpus suggests that these lower impulses naturally dissipated as her purity deepened. (1) The gentle departure — The San Shi, in her case, may not have been "cut out" but starved out by the absence of attachment. She did not force them to leave; they simply found no purchase in a woman who owned nothing, envied nothing, desired nothing. (2) The purity of her cultivation — Her path is often described as Su Xin (素心, a pure and unadorned heart) and Wu Wei (无为, effortless action). She did not cultivate through struggle but through non-grasping. The Yuan Ying (Nascent Soul) concept, with its terrifying replacement anxiety, does not feature in her legend. There is no second self gestated in her Dantian, no golden-faced stranger waiting to overwrite her identity. She remained He Qiong throughout. (3) "I" or "I" — She did not face the existential crisis of being replaced by a perfected version of herself. This may be the most radical difference between her path and the standard Xian trajectory: she never had to ask whether she was still herself, because she never stopped being who she was.
body.body_7: (1) Core attachment — She Xiangu's driving force was not the fear of death, nor the ambition to transcend the Three Realms. The legend presents her as fundamentally contented in her mortal life. The development of her immortal nature was not driven by a gnawing need, but by a quiet readiness to release her attachments when they naturally fell away. If she had a core drive, it was a deep and unassuming love for simplicity: for the mountains, for the herbs she gathered, for the solitude she chose. (2) Unspoken regrets — The classic material does not detail any personal loss or guilt. However, later folk readings occasionally suggest a subtle melancholy: that she outlived every member of her family, that she watched her parents grow old and die while she remained unchanged. The sources do not describe her grief, which may itself be the most telling detail—either she did not feel it, or she felt it so deeply that the legends chose silence over dramatization. (3) The unanswerable question — He Xiangu's legend asks a different question from the tragic cultivator's path. It does not ask whether Great Freedom is worth the price of humanity. It asks: what kind of woman walks out of her village, leaves behind everyone she has ever known, and feels no need to look back? Is she enlightened, or is she empty? The tradition offers her as a model of purity, but a modern reader may find her serenity more unsettling than any storm of emotion.
body.body_8: (1) Relationship with the Xian path — He Xiangu is a member of the Eight Immortals (Ba Xian), a fellowship of transcendent beings who roam the earthly realm to guide mortals and maintain cosmic balance. Within this group, she holds a unique position as the sole female immortal. Her relationship with her fellow Xian is presented as one of mutual respect and distinct purpose: where Lu Dongbin wields his sword against demonic chaos, and Li Tieguai carries his gourd of healing, He Xiangu offers stillness and quiet wisdom. (2) Contact with the Divine Path — The legend of her audience with Empress Wu Zetian is the most direct encounter with state authority. Summoned to the court of the only female emperor in Chinese history, He Xiangu is said to have demonstrated her supernatural lightness and her ability to live without food. The empress, impressed, offered her titles and wealth. He Xiangu declined them all, turned, and walked out of the palace. This act is often read as her refusal to exchange her natural state of freedom for any artificial status, even a divine decree. (3) The last thread to the mortal world — She is the daughter of a farming family, and that is the mortal identity that clings to her. Her name—He Xiangu, "Immortal Maiden He"—preserves her family name. In some local traditions, she is said to have returned to Zengcheng after her ascension, appearing as a vision to her descendants, ensuring that the He family line was blessed. (4) Encounters with the Yao path — The texts do not record any conflict with Yao (妖, demons or animal spirits). The medicine herbs she gathered in the mountains were for healing, not for hunting. (5) Encounters with the Mo path — No confrontation with demonic forces is recorded for He Xiangu. Her power, as the tradition presents it, was not the kind that sought out threats. She was never in the business of fighting.
body.body_9: (1) Current state — He Xiangu has achieved the state of Zhen Xian (True Immortal), fully ascended beyond the Three Realms and the Five Phases. Her name is inscribed in the celestial registry among the Eight Immortals. She is believed to roam the mortal world still, sometimes visible at festivals or in visions on Luofu Mountain, carrying her signature lotus flower or a bamboo colander. (2) Possible finality — For a Zhen Xian, there is no further stage. She has already achieved the ultimate goal of the Xian path: to be free from karmic debt, from the cycle of reincarnation, and from the reach of the Dao's reclaiming mechanism. The tradition does not speculate on a further fate. (3) Legacy for those who follow — The He family in Zengcheng treats her as an ancestral protector. The local temple in Zengcheng is a place of pilgrimage, and her legend is preserved in chapter-ballads, opera performances, and folk offerings. She left a written teaching to a disciple or not is unrecorded, but the emblem of the lotus flower she carries has become one of the most recognizable symbols of feminine immortality in the Daoist tradition.
body.body_10:
1. The He Xiangu Temple (何仙姑庙) in Zengcheng, Guangdong—the site of her family home, now a temple housing a statue of her in traditional garb, holding a lotus and a bamboo colander.  
2. A well in Zengcheng, from which she was said to have drunk on the day she ate the celestial peach; local tradition holds that its water brings longevity to those who draw it.  
3. The summit of Luofu Mountain, where a stone carved with her footprint is said to have been left when she ascended.  
4. Numerous folk paintings and woodblock prints from the Ming and Qing dynasties depicting her within the Eight Immortals fellowship, often placed at the forefront of processional banners for her association with purity and feminine virtue.
body.body_11: He Xiangu's path stands in notable contrast within the Eight Immortals fellowship. While Lü Dongbin's story is a long and painful struggle with pride and desire, and Li Tieguai is physically cursed by his own impatience with the lower cosmic self, He Xiangu is the only member who did not experience a catastrophic fall before her rise. Her story has no scene of failed alchemy, no betrayed master, no broken vow. Her simple path of pure-heartedness, emphasized in the Female Immortal Tradition, provides a significant point of comparison for understanding the diversity of Xian paths within the framework of "stealing creation" as defined in the Xian volume's general outline. This divergence in narrative tone demonstrates that the Xian path is not monolithic: some were driven by ambition, others were simply called, and a few, like He Xiangu, were offered the peach.

guide.guide_1: Imagine a girl in a small village in southern China, somewhere near modern-day Guangzhou. She's maybe sixteen. She's not especially ambitious, not particularly brilliant, not drowning in grief or motivation. She's just... a girl. She wakes up, eats breakfast, goes to gather herbs in the mountains. That's her life. One day, on the mountain, an old woman hands her a peach. The girl eats it. And from that moment on, her hunger never comes back. Not just hunger for food—hunger for anything. She stops wanting. She stops chasing. She stops aging. And she doesn't even realize that this is the beginning of her immortality until decades later, when everyone she grew up with has lines on their faces and she still looks like a teenager. That's He Xiangu. No sword, no alchemical crucible, no screaming contest with Heaven. Just a peach, and a girl who said yes.
guide.guide_2: If you've heard of the Eight Immortals, you've probably heard the simplified version: eight misfits who drank too much wine, played pranks, and sailed across the sea using their magical items. Fun image. But the real story of each immortal is its own novel-length tragedy or comedy, and He Xiangu's is the most quietly devastating of them all, precisely because it isn't loud. In Chinese folk culture, she's known as the maiden who ascended from Luofu Mountain, the girl who ate celestial food and never needed to eat again. The wholesome version. The gentle one. But the full story, if you read carefully, has a strange quality. She never seems to have had a moment of choice. She didn't decide to become immortal; she was handed immortality, and she accepted it with the same calm that she accepted everything else. The question nobody asks in the folk tales: was that acceptance a sign of enlightenment, or of something that was already missing?
guide.guide_3: The conventional cultivating hero has a story: he wants something desperately—revenge, power, the love of someone who died too young, the fear of his own death. He sees the Xian path as the answer to a gnawing hole inside him. He Xiangu's story has none of that. The source of her immortality is a gift: a peach from an immortal, a spirit in a dream who teaches her to eat mica powder. She does not fight for it and she does not earn it. She simply accepts. Now, you could read that as a beautiful message about the grace of fate, about how some people are chosen not because they deserve it but because their heart is pure. And that's the version you'll find in most temple pamphlets. But the unsettling thing is, He Xiangu never asks for anything—not before the peach, and certainly not after. She is not driven by the desire that fuels every conventional Xian's journey. The legend presents this as a calling, and the real question is what the calling quietly changed: did she become something less than human, or more than human, or simply something else that our vocabulary of "human" and "immortal" can't hold?
guide.guide_4: Let me walk you through the conventional Xian path. In the classic framework—the one followed by huge figures like Lü Dongbin and Zhang Sanfeng—the road to immortality is a long process of violent subtraction. You start with desire, you cut out one piece of your humanity at a time: first food, then sleep, then anger, then love of family, then fear, then the last shred of your mortal self. You eventually become a being with no wants, no regrets, no warmth. That's the deal. He Xiangu's path looks gentler on the outside, but it arrives at the same destination. She never had to fight for it, and that means she never had the experience of clinging to something and then being forced to let it go. She simply... didn't cling. She didn't lose her ability to love or feel; she just never developed a strong attachment in the first place. The tradition calls this "Su Xin" (pure heart). But think about what a "pure heart" really means: it means a heart that has never been scratched, never been stained, never been broken. It's not that she healed from suffering—it's that she never suffered. That sounds peaceful. But is it human? He Xiangu's story asks a question that the other Eight Immortals never raise: what is the value of a humanity that was never tested?
guide.guide_5: And yet she stayed in the world. That's the detail that keeps me up at night. After her ascension, He Xiangu remained among humans—not as a distant celestial, but as a living village girl who happened to never get older. She walked among her family, gathered herbs, tended to the sick. She watched her brothers and sisters grow gray, watched their children be born, watched those children grow old. She stayed. In that, she is almost more terrifying than the epic hero who leaves. She is like a clock that never moves while everything around her does. The tradition doesn't ask whether she felt pain watching her parents die. The tradition doesn't ask if she ever felt lonely when she was the only face in the village that didn't change. It simply records her acts: she healed the sick, she gave alms, she taught meditation. She did good. But what was she feeling? The story is silent. And that silence is the most honest thing about it. Maybe she didn't feel anything. Maybe she had become so pure, so aligned with the Dao, that loss no longer registered as loss. Maybe that's the point of her story: not that she was a perfect woman, but that she was a woman who became perfect by ceasing to feel the things that make us imperfect.
guide.guide_6: The legends barely mention her relationships. She had a family, but no dramatic reunion or betrayal. She served under Empress Wu Zetian, but the story is only a few lines: summoned, showed her lightness, offered a title, declined, left. No dialogue, no conflict, no emotional charge. The tradition does not preserve her interior life—that's the most consistent thing about her. She is the only one of the Eight Immortals whose biography reads like a weather report: serene, calm, uneventful. But think about the Eight Immortals fellowship itself: Lü Dongbin carries his sword-wielding arrogance, Li Tieguai his hunchback and his temper, Zhongli Quan his enormous belly and his laughter. They're characters. They have edges. He Xiangu is the one with no edges. That makes her hard to write about, but it also makes her essential. She is the stillness in the center of the storm. In a way, she is the purest symbol of the Eight Immortals: a woman who achieved transcendence not by fighting the world, but by being so light that the world simply let her slip through.
guide.guide_7: He Xiangu's story has no villain. No obstacle. No final exam. That's what makes her the hardest of the Eight Immortals for a modern audience to connect with. We are trained to value struggle: the hero who faces impossible odds and emerges triumphant. But what about the hero who simply steps aside? What about the woman who sits down by the river, eats a peach handed to her by a stranger, and lets the years flow past her like water? There is something deeply uncomfortable about her, if you look honestly. She doesn't want anything. She doesn't miss anything. She is pure, but purity is cold. Maybe that's the real lesson of her story: not that we should become like her, but that we should be grateful for our messy, hungry, imperfect attachment to life. The peach was free. But maybe we wouldn't want it if we understood what it really cost.

seo.meta_description: He Xiangu, the only woman among the Eight Immortals. Ascended not through struggle but through a single gift—a celestial peach. The quietest and perhaps most unsettling path to transcendence.
seo.og_title: He Xiangu: The Peasant Girl Who Became a True Immortal
seo.og_description: He Xiangu, the Immortal Maiden He, is the solitary female figure among China's Eight Immortals. Her path to transcendence was not marked by struggle or sword, but by a single peach and a heart so pure it never learned to cling.
seo.twitter_title: He Xiangu: The Eight Immortals' Quietest Member
seo.twitter_description: The only woman among the Eight Immortals, He Xiangu gained immortality by accepting a celestial peach. No battle, no tribulation—only a serene path that left her gentle but perhaps inhuman.

lore_entries.description: The Immortal Maiden He, the only female member of the Eight Immortals (Ba Xian). A Tang Dynasty peasant girl who achieved Xian-hood through a celestial peach and the ingestion of Yun Mu (mica powder), without undergoing the conventional stages of tribulation-driven cultivation.
A legendary fellowship of eight Xian who each achieved transcendence through a distinct path. They now roam the mortal world to guide souls and maintain cosmic balance.
Mica powder, a substance He Xiangu consumed after being taught by a spirit in a dream. It granted her lightness of body and an end to hunger, forming the core of her longevity.
A sacred Daoist peak in Guangdong Province, considered the site of He Xiangu's complete ascension. A stone carved with her footprint is said to remain at the summit.

Pure Heart; a concept in He Xiangu's legend describing her natural state of non-attachment and absence of desire—achieved not through struggle but through an inherent purity that never learned to cling.

faq_entries.question: Why is He Xiangu often depicted carrying a lotus or a bamboo colander?
faq_entries.answer: The lotus symbolizes purity and non-attachment (emerging unstained from the mud). The bamboo colander is a folk instrument said to have been her basket for gathering medicinal herbs, now an emblem of her healing and provision.

faq_entries.question: Did He Xiangu face the conventional tribulations described in Xian mythology, such as the Three Calamities or the Three Worms?
faq_entries.answer: No. The legends do not record her experiencing any of the standard tribulations. She achieved transcendence through a gift, not through theft from the cosmos, which may explain why the Dao's self-correcting mechanism never targeted her.

faq_entries.question: How did He Xiangu interact with Empress Wu Zetian?
faq_entries.answer: She was summoned to court, demonstrated her supernatural lightness and ability to live without food, was offered titles—and simply left. She is said to have refused all gifts and walked out of the imperial presence without visible emotion.

faq_entries.question: Where is He Xiangu's principal shrine?
faq_entries.answer: In Zengcheng, Guangdong Province, at the site of her family home. The temple is a major pilgrimage site, and a well associated with her legend is believed to grant longevity.
